name: Vibravox
description: Vibravox is a dataset compliant with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) containing audio recordings using five different body-conduction audio sensors: two in-ear microphones, two bone conduction vibration pickups, and a laryngophone. The dataset also includes audio data from an airborne microphone used as a reference. The Vibravox corpus contains 45 hours per sensor of speech samples and physiological sounds recorded by 188 participants under different acoustic conditions imposed by a high order ambisonics 3D spatializer. Annotations about the recording conditions and linguistic transcriptions are also included in the corpus.
creator: Julien Hauret, Malo Olivier, Thomas Joubaud, Christophe Langrenne, Sarah Poirée, Véronique Zimpfer, and Éric Bavu
publisher: Laboratoire de Mécanique des Structures et des Systèmes Couplés, Conservatoire national des arts et métiers, HESAM Université; French-German Research Institute of Saint-Louis (ISL)
citeAs: J. Hauret, M. Olivier, C. Langrenne, S. Poirée, and É. Bavu, 'vibravox (revision 071945b),' 2024. [Online]. Available: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Cnam-LMSSC/vibravox
rai:dataCollection: A total of 200 participants contributed to the dataset, with 188 retained after post-processing. Participants were recorded wearing six audio sensors simultaneously (five body-conduction sensors and one airborne reference microphone) using a Zoom F8n field recorder operating at 48 kHz and 32-bit resolution. Recordings were conducted under different acoustic conditions imposed by a high-order ambisonics 3D spatializer with a spherical array of 56 loudspeakers. The recording process consisted of four steps: speech-clean (participant reads sentences for 15 minutes), speechless-noisy (2 minutes 24 seconds of silence in noisy environment), speechless-clean (54 seconds in complete silence), and speech-noisy (54 seconds of speech in noisy environment).
rai:dataCollectionType: Physical data collection, Direct measurement, Experiments
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Out of 200 participants, 188 were retained after post-processing, with 6% of participants and 6.8% of pronounced sentences excluded. Issues included mispronounced sentences, sensors shifting from initial positions, occasional sensor malfunctions, and instances where a microphone was inadvertently left unequipped. In some cases, such as when a participant's ear canal was too small for the rigid in-ear microphone to achieve proper acoustic sealing, automatic filters were not triggered.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Audio recordings from six simultaneous sensors (five body-conduction sensors and one airborne reference microphone) recorded at 48 kHz and 32-bit resolution. Text data originated from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice. Ambient noise samples were sourced from Audio Set (focused on battlefield and industrial noise classes) and in-house recordings of concerts and street events in 3rd and 5th order ambisonics.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: A 20 Hz high-pass filter was uniformly applied to each acquisition channel to attenuate low-frequency noise and artifacts. For the speech-noisy and speechless-noisy subsets, audio recordings were spatialized using the ambitools library and rendered by a spherical array of 56 loudspeakers. Audio Set noise samples were spatialized using a plane wave model from random fixed positions uniformly distributed on the sphere. Voice Activity Detection (VAD) timestamps were extended by 0.6 seconds on both sides; in rare cases where adjusted timestamps exceeded original audio boundaries, audio was trimmed by 15 ms on the affected side.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Post-processing filtering comprised three automatic filters applied to the speech-clean subset: (1) Phoneme Error Rate filter discarding samples where PER > 10%; (2) SNR filter verifying sensor functioning by checking that SNR[i,j] = L_speech_50[i,j] - L_silence_50[i,j] > 1.5 dB; (3) sensitivity drift filter checking that L_speech_50[i,j] > L_silence_50[i]. The whisper-timestamped model was used as a key component for indicator extraction. The dataset was split by speaker with 80% in training, 10% in development/validation, and 10% in test set, ensuring no speaker overlap between splits. Signals were resampled to 16 kHz for model training.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Text utilized for participant readings originated from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice, further filtered to exclude proper names (except common first names, French town/region names, and country names), numbers, Greek letters, mathematical symbols, and syntactic errors. Common text normalization operations were applied (lowercasing, removing punctuation except apostrophes). Phonetic transcriptions using the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) with 33 French phonemes were generated using the text phonemizer of the CoML lab. Words unrecognized by the phonemizer underwent manual phonetic transcription.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Text phonemizer of the CoML lab (phonemizer library); whisper-timestamped model for word timestamp alignment and phoneme error rate computation
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Phoneme Error Rate (PER) was computed using the Levenshtein distance between the phonetic labeled transcription and the phonetic transcription derived from Whisper's output. Samples with PER > 10% were discarded to ensure high-quality labels for the speech-to-phonemes task. Manual phonetic transcription was performed for words unrecognized by the automatic phonemizer.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The corpus is publicly available online on HuggingFace under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license. The dataset is referenced as revision 071945b.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Gender and age of participants are recorded. Age statistics are provided: female participants mean age 25.9 years (range 19-59), male participants mean age 31.4 years (range 18-82). Voice recordings and physiological sounds (heart rate, breathing) are included. All necessary measures were taken to protect privacy and rights of participants in accordance with GDPR, including obtaining informed consent, clearly communicating the purpose of data collection, and ensuring anonymization and encryption of data during storage and analysis.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to advance research in body-conducted speech capture for robust communication in noisy environments, with potential applications in military operations, industrial settings, access control, and intelligence gathering. The dataset could enable voice commands for heavy machinery operation and monitoring of vital signs. A deliberate effort was made to recruit a diverse and gender-balanced group of participants to increase representativeness and inclusivity.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset is exclusively in French, restricting applicability to French-language research. The age distribution is skewed toward younger participants (median age 25 for females, 27 for males). The Lombard effect causes speakers to increase vocal effort in noisy conditions, meaning reported signal-to-external-noise ratios represent a lower bound on actual values. A 'one-size-fits-all' sensor design may not fit all ear canal anatomies, leading to acoustic sealing issues for some participants with in-ear microphones.
rai:dataLimitations: The speech-noisy subset primarily serves testing purposes as it lacks a clean reference under noisy conditions. Some sensors exhibit limited bandwidth (e.g., temple vibration pickup barely records speech above 1500 Hz, laryngophone coherence drops below 0.25 at 2000 Hz). The dataset is exclusively in French. Individual variance in noise transmission through devices and ear canal anatomy variations affect recording quality. The manufacturing process for some novel sensors is not yet stabilized. The dataset is not the largest BCM dataset available (45h37 per sensor vs. 128h for ESMB).
rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, and Validation for speech enhancement (bandwidth extension), automatic speech recognition (speech-to-phonemes), and speaker verification tasks. The speech-clean subset is the primary training resource. The speech-noisy subset serves primarily for testing. The speechless-clean subset is valuable for heart rate tracking, noise property analysis, and generating synthetic datasets with realistic physiological noise. Data augmentation can be applied by combining speechless-noisy segments with BCM utterances to simulate noisy scenarios while retaining a clean reference.
rai:annotatorDemographics: 188 participants (97 female, 91 male); female age range 19-59 years (mean 25.9, median 22); male age range 18-82 years (mean 31.4, median 27); overall age range 18-82 years (mean 28.55, median 25). A deliberate effort was made to recruit a diverse and gender-balanced group.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: whisper-timestamped model (speech-to-text engine based on Whisper with dynamic time warping for word timestamp alignment); text phonemizer of the CoML lab (IPA phonetic transcription)
